idiom_name: generator expressions plus itertools (C-level adapters) with a terminal consumer
implementation_notes: Python's replacement for the classic chain is the generator protocol: generator expressions and generator functions are lazy, and itertools supplies fast, memory-efficient iterator building blocks (map, filter, islice, accumulate, chain, groupby), so a pipeline can be expressed end to end without materializing a list per stage. What does not happen is loop fusion: every generator stage is a frame switch per element and only itertools primitives run at C level, so the practical rule is to lean on itertools for the hot steps and keep hand-written generator stages few. reduce or a small consumer function drives the single pass.
code_sketch:
from itertools import islice
adults = (p for p in people if p.age > 18)   # lazy generator
scores = map(lambda p: p.score, adults)      # itertools, C level
total = sum(islice(scores, 100))             # terminal: one pass
pitfalls: Generators are single-use: after one pass the pipeline is exhausted and iterating it again yields nothing, silently.
Each hand-written generator stage costs a frame switch per element; itertools.map/islice avoid it, and a plain for loop beats a chain of lambda stages in hot code.
Long generator chains keep their frame locals (and any open files) alive for their whole lifetime; close or scope them deliberately, since an abandoned generator defers cleanup to the GC.
